The evidence on whether standing desks help with weight loss is genuinely conflicting. Several high-credibility sources conclude that the calorie difference between standing and sitting is too small to produce meaningful weight loss: Harvard Health reports standing burns only about 88 calories/hour versus 80 while sitting, leading researchers to conclude a standing desk is "unlikely to help with weight loss or avoiding weight gain" [d1]. The Washington Post, citing a meta-analysis of over 50 studies, reports that standing burns only 0.15 extra calories per minute, which the lead researcher said is "probably not enough to help people lose weight" [d9]. Houston Methodist similarly states that a standing desk "won't help you lose weight," and that the small calorie difference is "unlikely to contribute to any weight loss or weight maintenance goals" [d10]. A Cochrane medical review cited by ABC News found insufficient high-quality evidence of benefit, with a co-author explicitly stating that "standing instead of sitting hardly increases energy expenditure, so we should not expect a sit-stand desk to help in losing weight" [d12]. The New York Times also reported that being upright is "unlikely to help us lose weight" based on a recent study [d11]. On the other side, Mayo Clinic research found that substituting standing for sitting for six hours a day could burn an extra 54 calories, which — assuming no increase in food intake — could equate to 5.5 pounds lost in one year and 22 pounds over four years [d6]. Some sources also argue that standing promotes additional incidental movement (shifting, pacing, stretching) that activates fat-burning enzymes and increases overall calorie expenditure through NEAT (non-exercise activity thermogenesis), potentially contributing to modest weight loss over time [d8, d5]. In summary, most credible evidence suggests standing desks alone are unlikely to produce significant weight loss, though they may help prevent weight gain and offer other health benefits; more optimistic projections depend on sustained long-duration standing and increased incidental movement [d1, d6, d9, d12].
